items.title: Point
items.explanation: A point is a precise location in space with no length, breadth, or height. It can be represented by a sharp pencil tip, the pointed end of a needle, or the tip of a compass. When three points are marked on paper (e.g., P, Q, R), they must be distinguished by capital letters to avoid confusion.

items.title: Line Segment
items.explanation: A line segment is a part of a line that has two distinct end points. It is the shortest path between two points (e.g., A and B). It is denoted by the capital letters of its endpoints, such as AB or BA.

items.title: Line
items.explanation: A line extends infinitely in both directions through any two given points. While a line segment has fixed ends, a line continues forever without an end. It is often denoted by lowercase letters like 'l' or 'm'. Any two points determine exactly one unique line.

items.title: Ray
items.explanation: A ray starts at one specific point (the starting point or initial point) and extends infinitely in one direction. It has only one end point. For example, a ray named AP starts at A and goes through P.

items.title: Angle
items.explanation: An angle is formed when two rays share a common starting point (the vertex). The vertex is the middle letter in naming an angle (e.g., Angle DBE), while the arms are named by a point on each ray and the vertex (e.g., Angle EBD).
